title: References and Aliasing
learningObjectives: Explain references as aliases to existing objects.
Initialize references and identify their binding.
Trace assignment through a reference alias.
Prevent references from outliving their targets.

understand.concept: A reference is an alias bound to an existing object. References normally must be initialized and cannot be reseated to another object.
understand.whyItMatters: References support safe parameter passing and convenient aliases without explicit dereference syntax.
understand.explain: Ensure the referred object's lifetime exceeds the reference's use.

examples.title: Alias with reference
examples.explanation: A reference aliases the original object.

examples.title: Reference initialization
examples.explanation: A reference must bind to an object when initialized.

examples.title: Two names same object
examples.explanation: Both alias access the same n.

examples.title: Reference cannot reseat
examples.code: int a=1,b=2;int& r=a;r=b;\n// r now assigns a from b; it does not bind to b
examples.explanation: Assignment through a reference changes the referred object.

examples.title: Const reference
examples.code: const int& view=value;\n// reading view is allowed; assigning through it is not
examples.explanation: A const reference provides read-only access.

practise.guidedTask: For References and Aliasing, draw the object and pointer/reference relationships for every example. Mark owner, target, constness, lifetime, validity of access, and any operation that could invalidate the pointer or reference.
practise.independentTask: Write a focused C++ exercise for References and Aliasing. Demonstrate at least three cases, including a safe usage and a boundary/invalid case explained in comments but not executed. State who owns the resource and when each object/view is valid.
hints: Draw the pointer/reference and its target object.
Mark whether the object is alive and who owns it.
Check nullptr and bounds before access.
Consider invalidation, deletion and scope exit.
Use standard containers or smart pointers when they express ownership more safely.

questions.explanation: A reference must bind to an object.
Reference assignment writes to the alias target.
References remain bound to their original object.
const reference disallows mutation through it.
